topics.title: Completed actions
topics.description: 了 for what just happened, 過 for what you've ever done

guide.intro: A1 introduced 了 briefly. A2 is where it really earns its keep. There are also two siblings to learn — 過 (experience) and 還沒 (not yet) — that round out talking about the past.

sections.text: 了 — completed action
Tack 了 onto a verb to mark that the action is finished. It's the closest thing Mandarin has to a past tense, but technically it's an aspect marker — the action is complete, not necessarily long ago.

rows.source: 我 吃 飯。
我 吃 了 飯。
他 來 了。

sections.text: Negation: 還沒 (not yet)
Don't pair 了 with 不/沒. To say "haven't done it", drop 了 and use 還沒 (hái méi):

rows.source: 我 還沒 吃。
他 還沒 來。

sections.text: 過 — experience marker
過 (guò) tags a verb as "have you ever done this in your life?" — it's about experience, not completion. Compare:

rows.source: 我 吃 過 北京 烤鴨。
我 吃 了 北京 烤鴨。

sections.text: Rule of thumb: 了 = the action is wrapped up. 過 = at some point in your life this happened. They occasionally co-occur but you'll mostly pick one.

lessons.title: 了 — completed action
lessons.description: 了 marks a completed action, not English past tense.

exercises.prompt: What does the 了 in "我 吃 了" signal?
exercises.explanation: 了 (le) marks completion — the eating happened and is done. It is NOT a tense marker.

exercises.prompt: "下 雨 了" most naturally means:

guide.intro: Real Chinese shopping is fast and friendly. Three phrases get you 80% of the way there: 多少錢 (how much), 太貴了 (too expensive), and 給我 (give me).

sections.text: Money words
Spoken Chinese uses 塊 (kuài) for the main currency unit; written and formal Chinese uses 元 (yuán). They're the same value — like "buck" vs "dollar". 毛 (máo) and 分 (fēn) are tenths and hundredths.

topics.title: Comparisons
topics.description: A is bigger than B — the 比 pattern

guide.intro: English uses "-er" or "more" for comparisons. Mandarin uses 比 (bǐ) — a single particle that does the same job, with a fixed word order: A 比 B + adjective.

sections.text: Basic pattern: A 比 B + adjective

rows.source: 我 比 他 高。
蘋果 比 香蕉 便宜。
今天 比 昨天 熱。

sections.text: Don't add 很 / 不 / 是 to a 比 sentence. "我 比 他 很 高" is wrong — drop 很. The comparison itself does the work.
Even more: 更
Add 更 (gèng, "even more") before the adjective when comparing to an already-strong baseline:

rows.source: 他 比 我 更 高。
rows.translation: He is even taller than me.

sections.text: The most: 最
最 (zuì) before an adjective means "the most". No 比 needed — it's a superlative.

rows.source: 他 最 高。
我 最 喜歡 茶。

sections.text: Negative: A 沒有 B + adjective
To say "A is NOT as ___ as B", flip to 沒有 (méi yǒu, "doesn't have"):

rows.source: 我 沒有 他 高。
rows.translation: I am not as tall as him.

topics.title: Connecting ideas
topics.description: And, but, because, so — stitch sentences together

guide.intro: Up to now most sentences have been one thought. A2 is where you start chaining: "I went and then I ate", "It rained but I went", "I'm tired because I worked". Mandarin makes this easy — a small set of connectors does most of the heavy lifting.

sections.text: 然後 — and then
然後 (rán hòu) chains two events in time. Use it to narrate sequences.

rows.source: 我 起床，然後 吃 早飯。
rows.translation: I get up, and then I eat breakfast.

sections.text: 但是 / 可是 — but
Both mean "but" with no real difference; 可是 is a touch more conversational.

rows.source: 我 想 去，但是 我 沒 時間。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng qù, dànshì wǒ méi shíjiān.
rows.translation: I want to go, but I don't have time.

sections.text: 因為...所以 — because...so
Mandarin often uses both halves where English uses just one ("I'm tired BECAUSE I worked" → 因為 我 工作 了，所以 我 很 累).

rows.source: 因為 下雨，所以 我 沒 去。
rows.pinyin: Yīnwèi xià yǔ, suǒyǐ wǒ méi qù.
rows.translation: Because it was raining, (so) I didn't go.

sections.text: You can drop one half if context is clear: "因為 下雨，我 沒 去" works too. The full pair just sounds slightly more emphatic.
或者 vs 還是 — both mean "or"
Easy mix-up. 或者 (huò zhě) goes in statements ("I want tea or coffee"). 還是 (hái shi) goes in questions ("Do you want tea or coffee?").

rows.translation: I want to drink tea or coffee. (statement)

rows.pinyin: Nǐ xiǎng hē chá háishi kāfēi?
